t: Micro-DDS: What Micro-DDS Is: DDS for Small Things
title: Micro-DDS: What Micro-DDS Is: DDS for Small Things
description: DDS is the industrial pub/sub standard — decentralized, QoS-rich, real-time — and Micro-DDS (the XRCE-DDS profile, eProsima's implementation) brings it to microcontrollers and constrained links. A tiny XRCE client on a Cortex-M talks through an agent to the full DDS global data space: the sensor node publishes, the flight computer subscribes, with the same reliability and deadline policies as the big systems. It is how resource-starved edges join grown-up middleware instead of speaking ad-hoc serial protocols.

title: Micro-DDS: XRCE-DDS: The Client/Agent Pattern
description: XRCE splits the work: the tiny client on the microcontroller speaks a compact binary protocol over serial or UDP to the agent, and the agent — running on a capable host — participates in full DDS on the client's behalf. The client stays small (tens of KB); the agent does discovery, matching, and QoS. This is the right division of labor: the edge stays lean, the infrastructure stays smart.

t: Micro-DDS: QoS on a Diet: What Survives
title: Micro-DDS: QoS on a Diet: What Survives
description: Constrained DDS keeps the QoS that matters: reliability (best-effort vs reliable with the agent buffering), durability for late joiners, deadlines, and liveliness — implemented within the client's memory budget. The art is choosing: reliable delivery costs buffers the microcontroller may not have, so critical topics get reliability and telemetry stays best-effort. Every QoS choice is a memory budget line.

title: Micro-DDS: Determinism: Time-Triggered Options
description: Some systems need not just fast but predictable: time-triggered DDS profiles schedule transmissions in fixed slots, so worst-case latency is computed, not hoped. Space and flight systems live here — the bus schedule is part of the safety case. Micro-DDS deployments in these domains pair the middleware with schedule analysis: every topic's period, deadline, and jitter budget documented and verified.

t: Micro-DDS: Your First Talker: Client to Data Space
title: Micro-DDS: Your First Talker: Client to Data Space
description: The hello-world: an XRCE client on a dev board publishes a counter; the agent on the laptop bridges it to DDS; a subscriber prints it. The same code, pointed at a flight computer's agent, becomes flight telemetry. The lesson is the architecture's transparency — the application does not know or care where the agent lives.

title: Micro-DDS: Discovery: Finding Each Other
description: DDS discovery is decentralized — no broker — using multicast or configured peers to find matching publishers and subscribers. On constrained networks, discovery is tuned: static peer lists instead of multicast storms, the agent handling discovery for its clients. In space links with minutes of delay, discovery is preconfigured, not dynamic. The network's constraints shape the discovery strategy.

t: Micro-DDS: Space Profile: DTN and Long Delays
title: Micro-DDS: Space Profile: DTN and Long Delays
description: Space networks break terrestrial assumptions: minutes of light-delay, scheduled contacts, intermittent links. DDS profiles for space (and the DTN — delay-tolerant networking — underneath) use store-and-forward, custody transfer, and contact planning. Micro-DDS's small footprint suits flight computers; the space profile suits the physics. Together they are how modern smallsats talk — and how lunar networks will.

t: Micro-DDS: Defensive Uses: The Trusted Bus
title: Micro-DDS: Defensive Uses: The Trusted Bus
description: Micro-DDS's defensive value is a trustworthy nervous system for uncrewed vehicles and field systems: authenticated participants, QoS-guaranteed command delivery, deadline-monitored telemetry — on hardware too small for enterprise middleware. A UGV whose command link has proven deadlines and authenticated publishers is a system the operator can trust at distance. The bus becomes part of the safety case.

title: Micro-DDS: Reliability: What 'Reliable' Costs
description: Reliable QoS means the agent buffers unacked samples and retransmits — memory and bandwidth spent for certainty. On constrained links, teams budget it: commands reliable, high-rate telemetry best-effort, with the sequence numbers letting subscribers detect gaps. The engineering is explicit about the trade: certainty has a price, paid in buffers.

title: Micro-DDS: Debugging: The Silent Subscriber
description: DDS debugging classics: the subscriber that never receives (QoS mismatch — check compatibility), discovery that never completes (multicast blocked), and the agent that drops clients (resource limits). The tools are the DDS spy (list the data space), QoS compatibility reporting, and the agent's logs. The first question is always: do they see each other? Then: do they agree?

t: Micro-DDS: Security: DDS-Security on Small Devices
title: Micro-DDS: Security: DDS-Security on Small Devices
description: DDS-Security brings authentication, access control, and encryption to the data space — and the XRCE profile carries it to constrained devices via the agent. The plugins (PKI auth, crypto, access control) are the same model as SROS2's. Key provisioning for fleets of devices is the operational challenge; the answer is manufacturing-time provisioning with rotation. An unauthenticated bus is a remote-control interface for anyone on the network.

title: Micro-DDS: Performance: Latency Budgets
description: Micro-DDS deployments live on budgets: sensor-to-actuator latency decomposed into bus hops, each with a deadline. The measurement is end-to-end with hardware timestamps — not estimates. Tuning is buffer sizes, thread priorities, and (for time-triggered) slot maps. The budget document is the performance contract, reviewed when anything changes.
key_facts: Measured p99 must fit the budget

title: Micro-DDS: Testing: Conformance and Interop
description: DDS's strength is standards: conformance tests verify the implementation, interop events verify vendors work together. Micro-DDS programs add the constrained layer: client/agent protocol tests, resource-exhaustion tests (what happens at the buffer limit?), and long-soak tests for leaks. A middleware that fails gracefully under exhaustion is a middleware you can field.

t: Micro-DDS: Real-World Pattern: Flight Computer Bus
title: Micro-DDS: Real-World Pattern: Flight Computer Bus
description: A complete pattern: a smallsat's flight computer runs the steward; payload heralds publish telemetry in attested slots; the ground station subscribes through the data space during contacts. Commands go reliable with custody; telemetry goes best-effort with gap detection. The bus schedule is part of the mission's safety case, reviewed alongside the flight software.
